blocks.content: Not every operating system is built for the same purpose. The system running a giant bank mainframe, the one on your laptop, the one inside a car airbag controller, and the one spread across a data centre are all operating systems, but they are shaped very differently by the jobs they do.

Over the history of computing, several distinct types emerged, each solving the problem of its era. Knowing these types gives you a map of the whole field and shows why an operating system is always a product of what it needs to achieve.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308715-21007505.png
1. Why There Are Different Types

Operating systems differ because their goals differ. Some need to squeeze maximum work out of expensive hardware, some need to serve many people at once, and some need to react to the physical world within a fraction of a second.

These goals pull the design in different directions. A system built to guarantee split second responses looks nothing like one built to grind through huge batches of work overnight. The types below are really different answers to the question: what matters most here?

["Different operating systems have different goals","Some maximise hardware use, some serve many users, some react fast","Each goal pulls the design in a different direction","The types are answers to what matters most for that use"]

Some maximise hardware use, some serve many users, some react fast

blocks.content: 2. Batch Operating Systems

Batch systems were among the earliest. In the early days computers were rare and precious, so users could not interact with them directly. Instead they submitted jobs, and the system collected these into a batch and ran them one after another.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308715-393809202.png

There was no interaction while a job ran, you simply submitted it and came back later for the results. The goal was to keep the expensive machine busy at all times, wasting no idle moments. Batch ideas still live on today in large scheduled jobs that run without anyone watching.
["Among the earliest operating systems","Jobs are collected into a batch and run one by one","No interaction while a job runs","The goal was to keep expensive hardware always busy"]
items: Among the earliest operating systems
Jobs are collected into a batch and run one by one
No interaction while a job runs
The goal was to keep expensive hardware always busy

blocks.title: The old post office
blocks.content: A batch system is like dropping a form in a box and coming back tomorrow for the result. You cannot chat with the clerk while it is processed, you just submit and wait. Efficient for the clerk, but no back and forth.
3. Time Sharing Operating Systems
Time sharing systems were a leap forward. Instead of running one job to completion, the system rapidly switches the processor among many users and programs, giving each a small slice of time in turn.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308944-855113236.png

Because the switching is so fast, each user feels like they have the machine to themselves, even though many share it. This is the direct ancestor of the interactive systems we use today, where you type and get an immediate response. Your laptop is, at heart, a time sharing system.

["The processor is shared among many users and programs","Each gets a rapid slice of time in turn","Fast switching makes each user feel alone on the machine","The ancestor of the interactive systems we use today"]
items: The processor is shared among many users and programs
Each gets a rapid slice of time in turn
Fast switching makes each user feel alone on the machine
The ancestor of the interactive systems we use today

blocks.title: One tutor, many students
blocks.content: A skilled tutor helping a room of students spends a few seconds with each, then moves on, cycling around fast. Each student feels attended to. Time sharing does the same with the processor and its users.
4. Real Time Operating Systems
A real time operating system, often shortened to RTOS, is built around one demand: responding within a strict time limit. It is not about being fast on average, it is about never missing a deadline.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308945-129333689.png

These run where late is as bad as wrong: an airbag controller, a pacemaker, an aircraft control system, a factory robot. When a sensor fires, the response must come before the deadline, every single time. Predictability matters more than raw speed or convenience.

["Built to respond within a strict time limit","Never missing a deadline matters more than average speed","Used in airbags, pacemakers, aircraft, and robots","Predictability is valued above convenience"]
items: Built to respond within a strict time limit
Never missing a deadline matters more than average speed
Used in airbags, pacemakers, aircraft, and robots
Predictability is valued above convenience

blocks.title: Hard and soft deadlines
blocks.content: Real time systems come in two flavours. Hard real time, like an airbag, must never miss a deadline. Soft real time, like video streaming, tries hard but can tolerate the occasional slip.
5. Distributed Operating Systems

A distributed operating system ties together many separate computers so they behave, as much as possible, like one system. The machines are connected over a network and cooperate to share work and resources.

The goal is to make the collection feel unified, so a user or program does not have to worry about which specific machine is doing what. This is the world of large clusters and data centres, where huge tasks are spread across many computers working together.

["Ties many separate computers into one cooperating system","The machines are connected over a network","Work and resources are shared across the machines","Common in large clusters and data centres"]
items: Ties many separate computers into one cooperating system
The machines are connected over a network
Work and resources are shared across the machines
Common in large clusters and data centres

blocks.title: A team acting as one
blocks.content: A distributed system is like a large team where the work is split among members, but to the outside it looks like a single, capable unit. The coordination happens behind the scenes.
6. Embedded Operating Systems

An embedded operating system runs inside a device that is not thought of as a computer at all: a microwave, a smart watch, a router, a washing machine, a car dashboard. It is small, focused, and tailored to that one device.

Because the hardware is limited and the job is fixed, these systems are stripped down to just what the device needs, and they often run for years without ever being restarted. Many of them are also real time, since the devices must react promptly to their surroundings.
["Runs inside devices not seen as computers","Small, focused, and tailored to one device","Stripped down to fit limited hardware","Often runs for years without a restart"]

blocks.content: 7. Mobile Operating Systems

Mobile operating systems power phones and tablets. They descend from the desktop systems but are reshaped around touch input, small screens, always on connectivity, and the tight energy budget of a battery.

They pay special attention to battery life, aggressively managing which apps can run in the background, and they are built around app stores and strong per app permissions. Android and the system on the iPhone are the dominant examples in daily life.
["Power phones and tablets","Reshaped around touch, small screens, and connectivity","Manage battery life by controlling background apps","Built around app stores and per app permissions"]

blocks.content: 8. Comparing the Types
Laying the types side by side makes their differences clear. Each one optimises for a different priority, and that priority shapes everything about how it is built.

9. Types Overlap in Practice
These categories are not rigid boxes. A single real system often belongs to several types at once, blending their ideas as needed.

The system in a modern car, for example, is embedded because it lives inside the vehicle, and real time because it must react to sensors instantly. Your laptop is a time sharing system that also borrows heavily from mobile ideas for battery and app management. The types are lenses, not walls.
